mythsVsFacts.myth: One high reading diagnoses hypertension.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Diagnosis requires repeated measurements and GP assessment.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Pharmacy starts blood pressure treatment.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Long-term treatment is GP-led.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Home monitors replace professional checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Both have roles — discuss readings with a clinician.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Caffeine does not affect readings.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Rest before measurement; caffeine can temporarily raise readings.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Only elderly people need checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Risk factors matter at any adult age.

mythsVsFacts.myth: High blood pressure always causes symptoms.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Hypertension is often silent.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Every check is free for everyone.
mythsVsFacts.fact: NHS eligibility varies by pathway.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Stress readings are always wrong.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Repeat measurement or ABPM may be needed.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Pharmacy replaces ambulatory monitoring.
mythsVsFacts.fact: ABPM may be recommended by GP after screening.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Lifestyle changes never help.
mythsVsFacts.fact: They are often first-line alongside medical review.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Blood Pressure Checks replaces all GP care.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Blood Pressure Checks complements GP services — chronic and complex conditions remain with your GP.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Every patient automatically qualifies for Blood Pressure Checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Individual clinical assessment confirms suitability for blood pressure checks.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Blood Pressure Checks is always free.
mythsVsFacts.fact: NHS eligibility and commissioning determine cost — private blood pressure checks may incur disclosed fees.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Walk-in guarantees immediate Blood Pressure Checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Booking may be required; clinical assessment always precedes supply.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Online research removes the need for Blood Pressure Checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Personalised assessment and supply decisions require a pharmacist consultation.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Blood Pressure Checks treats emergencies.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Emergencies need 999 or A&E — blood pressure checks is not an emergency service.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Side effects from Blood Pressure Checks should be ignored.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Report side effects promptly to the pharmacy or GP.

mythsVsFacts.myth: All pharmacies offer identical Blood Pressure Checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Commissioning, training and private service menus vary locally.

mythsVsFacts.myth: No follow-up is needed after Blood Pressure Checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Safety-netting and review are essential parts of safe care.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Blood Pressure Checks always includes medicine supply.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Advice-only outcomes are valid when supply is not clinically appropriate.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Pharmacists are not qualified for Blood Pressure Checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: GPhC-registered pharmacists deliver blood pressure checks under clinical governance.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Blood Pressure Checks is the same as a GP appointment.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Blood Pressure Checks operates within defined pharmacy scope with referral when needed.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Sharing Blood Pressure Checks medicines is acceptable.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Prescription medicines are individualised — never share.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Blood Pressure Checks needs no preparation.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Some appointments require specific preparation — confirm at booking.

mythsVsFacts.myth: NHS and private Blood Pressure Checks are identical.
mythsVsFacts.fact: NHS pathways have eligibility criteria; private scope may differ.

faqLibrary.question: Can a pharmacy diagnose high blood pressure?
faqLibrary.answer: No — pharmacy checks screen for raised readings; diagnosis remains with your GP. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: How often should I have my blood pressure checked?
faqLibrary.answer: Frequency depends on age, risk factors and previous readings. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: What should I do before my check?
faqLibrary.answer: Rest five minutes, wear loose sleeves, avoid caffeine for 30 minutes if possible. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: What if my reading is high?
faqLibrary.answer: Raised readings may prompt repeat measurement, home monitoring advice or GP referral. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: What are systolic and diastolic numbers?
faqLibrary.answer: Systolic is pressure when the heart beats; diastolic when it rests — measured in mmHg. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Do I need an appointment for Blood Pressure Checks?
faqLibrary.answer: Booking ahead for Blood Pressure Checks ensures adequate consultation time. Walk-in availability varies by pharmacy and season — call to confirm same-day capacity.

faqLibrary.question: Is Blood Pressure Checks free on the NHS?
faqLibrary.answer: NHS-funded Blood Pressure Checks is free where the service is commissioned and you meet eligibility criteria. Private blood pressure checks may incur a disclosed fee confirmed before supply.

faqLibrary.question: How long does a Blood Pressure Checks appointment take?
faqLibrary.answer: Blood Pressure Checks consultations typically take 15–45 minutes depending on assessment complexity, counselling depth and whether tests or supply are involved.

faqLibrary.question: Who is eligible for Blood Pressure Checks?
faqLibrary.answer: Eligibility for Blood Pressure Checks depends on clinical criteria, age, medical history and local NHS commissioning. Suitability is confirmed individually — not assumed at booking.

faqLibrary.question: What should I bring to my Blood Pressure Checks appointment?
faqLibrary.answer: Bring a complete medicines list, allergy history, relevant test results, travel itinerary if applicable, and photo ID for NHS or controlled services.

faqLibrary.question: Can I speak to a pharmacist before booking Blood Pressure Checks?
faqLibrary.answer: Yes — a brief phone triage helps confirm whether Blood Pressure Checks is appropriate, explains fees or NHS eligibility, and sets preparation expectations.

faqLibrary.question: What if I am not eligible for Blood Pressure Checks?
faqLibrary.answer: If Blood Pressure Checks is not suitable, the pharmacist signposts you to GP, NHS 111, sexual health services or urgent care with documented advice.

faqLibrary.question: How much does private Blood Pressure Checks cost?
faqLibrary.answer: Private blood pressure checks fees vary by pharmacy and service complexity. Costs are explained before supply — ask for a clear quote at booking.

faqLibrary.question: What happens during a Blood Pressure Checks consultation?
faqLibrary.answer: The pharmacist reviews history, confirms consent, assesses suitability, explains options with risks and benefits, and documents agreed next steps.

faqLibrary.question: When should I see a GP instead of Blood Pressure Checks?
faqLibrary.answer: Persistent, severe or worsening symptoms, pregnancy complications, systemic illness and emergency presentations need GP or urgent care — not blood pressure checks alone.

faqLibrary.question: Can I use Blood Pressure Checks for my child?
faqLibrary.answer: Paediatric blood pressure checks depends on age limits per pathway. Contact the pharmacy to confirm guardian requirements and commissioned paediatric scope.

faqLibrary.question: What follow-up is needed after Blood Pressure Checks?
faqLibrary.answer: Follow safety-netting advice, attend booked reviews, and contact the pharmacy or GP if symptoms persist, side effects occur or concerns arise.

faqLibrary.question: How do I book Blood Pressure Checks at the pharmacy?
